Parcel & Pine Insights
Report · August 2026
Product & Digital
App search fails customers who say “couch” — synonyms and typos cause 61% of null results
The app still runs on the old search index that web moved off last year. Porting web's synonym and typo handling to the app is worth about $5M a year.
By Priya Natarajan & Aisha Rahman
Published Aug 27, 2026
Data Jun 1 – Jul 31, 2026 · 12 usability sessions Jul 13–17
“I typed couch and it showed me covers. So I figured you don't sell couches and went to look somewhere else.” Participant P7, Android, sofa task — usability session, July 15
The short version
App search does noticeably worse than web on every quality metric. 8.7% of app queries return nothing (web: 5.2%). Top-3 click-through is 31% (web: 38%), and 22% of searches are reformulated (web: 15%).
Most nulls are vocabulary problems, not catalogue gaps. Synonym mismatches (“couch” vs “sofa”, “comforter” vs “duvet”) cause 34% of null results and misspellings cause 27%. Only 18% are for things we don't sell.
Usability sessions show why it matters. 7 of 12 participants typed “couch” first, and 4 of those 7 concluded we don't sell sofas.
Recommendation: port web's 412-pair synonym list and typo tolerance to the app index by October 15, ahead of peak. That recovers about $5.1M a year (range $2.0–8.0M) while the full migration to the v2 search service is pulled forward to Q1 2027.

01 App search is worse than web on all three quality measures, and has been all summer
Search matters more in the app than anywhere else. 44% of app sessions include a search, compared with 29% on web.
We analysed 9.8 million app queries from 4.1 million search sessions across June and July. We tracked the three metrics the Search & Discovery squad already uses for web. Null-result rate is the share of queries that return zero products. Top-3 click-through is the share of queries where the customer clicks one of the first three results. Reformulation rate is the share of queries followed within 60 seconds by a different query with no click in between. The app was worse than web on all three.
The app trails web on nulls, top-3 clicks and reformulations
Search quality metrics by platform, Jun–Jul 2026 · % of queries
[Chart: column]
App (iOS + Android): Null rate 8.7%; Top-3 CTR 31%; Reformulation 22%
Web: Null rate 5.2%; Top-3 CTR 38%; Reformulation 15%
Source: dw.fct_search_queries (app n = 9.8M queries; web n = 14.6M queries). Higher is better for click-through only.
This is not a seasonal blip. The app's weekly null rate stayed between 8.3% and 9.1% for the whole period and never came near the 5% target the squad set for web in 2025. The reason is technical. When web moved to the v2 search service in October 2025, it gained a curated synonym dictionary and fuzzy matching. The app still queries the v1 index, which matches exact tokens after stemming only. 1
The app null rate has stayed above 8% every week, far from the 5% target

[Chart: line]

02 Six in ten null results are customers using a different word, or misspelling ours
We have what these customers want. We just don't recognise the words they use for it.
We took a stratified random sample of 3,000 null-result app queries and hand-coded each one. Two coders worked on the sample and agreed 91% of the time (κ = 0.86). Synonym mismatches were the largest group, followed by misspellings. Together they account for 61% of nulls. Queries for products we genuinely don't carry, such as appliances and outdoor grills, are only 18%.
Synonyms and typos explain 61% of app null results
Root cause of null-result queries, hand-coded sample (n = 3,000) · % of null queries
[Chart: bar]
Share of nulls: Synonym / vocabulary mismatch 34%; Misspelling 27%; Not in catalogue 18%; Over-specified attributes 13%; Other / unclear 8%
“Over-specified” means valid attribute combinations the v1 index cannot match, e.g. “green velvet 3 seater”. Source: coded sample from dw.fct_search_queries.

The pattern is consistent. Our catalogue uses trade and UK-leaning terms (sofa, duvet, cushion, bedside table), while many US customers use everyday words (couch, comforter, throw pillow, nightstand). Web already maps all of these pairs. The app maps none of them.
03 In the lab, a failed first search reads as “they don't sell it”
The usability sessions show what the logs can't: a null result does not look like a search problem to customers. It looks like a missing product.
Aisha Rahman ran 12 moderated remote sessions (6 iOS, 6 Android; 8 existing customers and 4 non-customers who shop online for furniture). Each participant did three search tasks on a production build. We did not coach them on wording.
7 of 12 participants typed “couch” first when asked to find a sofa
First query typed for the task “Find a three-seat sofa under $1,200” · participants (n = 12)
[Chart: column]
Participants: couch 7; sofa 3; sectional 1; loveseat 1
Source: moderated usability study, Jul 13–17, 2026 (Aisha Rahman). The single “sectional” participant also got zero results.
Task outcomes across the 12 sessions
| | Task | Completed | Median time | What got in the way
| Find a three-seat sofa under $1,200 | 8 / 12 | 2m 40s | “couch” returned only covers; 4 of 7 gave up
| Find a king-size comforter | 7 / 12 | 3m 05s | 0 results for “comforter”; 3 found duvets by browsing Bedding
| Find a rug that fits an 8×10 room | 10 / 12 | 1m 50s | “8x10 rug” works; “8 by 10 rug” returned nothing
Why this matters more than the null rate suggests
Nine of the 12 participants said they would expect a competitor's app to “just know” that couch means sofa. When search failed, none of them tapped the “Browse categories” link on the empty-results screen, because it sits below the fold. The empty state is effectively a dead end.
04 Fixing vocabulary nulls is worth about $5M a year
Sessions that hit a null result convert at a third of the rate of sessions where the customer reformulated and then clicked.
App sessions that hit a null result convert at 1.3%
Session conversion by search outcome, app, Jun–Jul 2026 · % of sessions
[Chart: bar]
Conversion: Top-3 click 7.4%; Lower-rank click 5.1%; Reformulated + click 4.2%; Null result 1.3%; No search 2.9%
Descriptive, not causal: intent differs between groups. The sizing below uses the conservative “reformulated, then clicked” rate as the counterfactual. Source: dw.fct_search_queries, dw.fct_app_sessions.
In a typical month, 2.05M app search sessions include 238k (11.6%) that hit at least one null. Synonyms and typos cause 61% of those, or 145k sessions. We assume the fix resolves 75% of them (109k sessions). If those sessions go on to convert like “reformulated, then clicked” sessions (4.2% instead of 1.3%), that adds about 3,160 orders a month. At the app AOV of $134, that is $423k a month, or about $5.1M a year . Our low case (50% resolved, converting at 3.0%) gives $2.0M. Our high case (90% resolved, converting at 5.1%) gives $8.0M. None of these figures include the likely gain in top-3 click-through, and none account for peak, when app search volume roughly doubles.
Caveat
This is an opportunity estimate, not a measured effect. We will confirm it by releasing the synonym port behind a 50/50 flag for two weeks in October. The pre-registration is already drafted (see the experimentation playbook).
05 Recommendations
Port web's synonym dictionary (412 pairs) to the app's v1 index. Search Platform estimates 1.5 sprints, and it removes the largest class of nulls. Owner: Search & Discovery squad · By: Oct 15, 2026 (behind a 50/50 flag)
Turn on edit-distance-1 typo tolerance for queries of 5 characters or more. This covers the most common misspellings with low false-match risk. Owner: Search Platform · By: Oct 15, 2026
Redesign the empty-results screen. Show “Did you mean…” and the top three categories above the fold. Owner: App squad with Aisha Rahman · By: Nov 6, 2026 (before Black Friday code freeze)
Move the app to the v2 search service in Q1 2027 instead of Q3. This retires the dual-index maintenance cost for good. Owner: Head of Digital Product · Decision by: Sep 30, 2026 planning
Add null-rate, top-3 CTR and reformulation to the weekly app scorecard. Owner: Jonah Feld · By: Sep 15, 2026
Methodology
Log analysis
All US app and web search queries from Jun 1 to Jul 31, 2026, excluding bot-flagged traffic (0.9%) and internal accounts. A “session” is a 30-minute inactivity window. Metrics follow the Search & Discovery squad's definitions (dw.fct_search_queries, v3). Root-cause coding used a stratified random sample of 3,000 null queries, weighted by volume decile, coded independently by two analysts (κ = 0.86), with disagreements resolved by discussion.
Usability study
12 moderated remote sessions, 45 minutes each, recruited via UserInterviews. 8 existing customers and 4 non-customers; 6 iOS and 6 Android. Same three tasks for everyone, with the task order rotated. The sessions show how and why search fails. They are too small a sample to estimate how often it happens.
Opportunity sizing
Monthly averages from Jun–Jul. Counterfactual conversion is taken from observed outcome groups, which are affected by self-selection, so we report a range and will validate with an experiment.
Limitations
Two summer months including Pine Days. Assumes app AOV ($134) is unchanged. Does not cover voice search (under 1% of queries) or the marketplace channel.
1 The v1 index applies Porter stemming, so “sofas” matches “sofa”, but it has no synonym expansion and no fuzzy matching. See Search Platform's ADR-031 (Oct 2025) for the web migration.

More shoppers know us; fewer pick us once they compare
Brand tracker wave 4 (June 2026, n = 2,421). Aided awareness has risen 6 points in a year, mostly from social. But we turn consideration into preference worse than any competitor, and the gap is perceived quality.
By Lena Kowalski
Published Aug 20, 2026
Fieldwork Jun 8–22, 2026
“They're my go-to for things I need fast, like a lamp or bath towels. For a sofa I'd want something I trust will last ten years, and I'm not sure I'd get that from them.” Wave 4 open-end, considers Parcel & Pine but prefers Competitor B (female, 38, Chicago)
The short version
Awareness is up to 44%, from 38% in wave 1. The +3-point rise since wave 3 is statistically significant. A third of recently-aware shoppers first heard of us through social ads.
We lose shoppers between consideration and preference. Only 36% of those who consider us prefer us, the lowest conversion of the four brands (Competitor A: 49%).
Perceived quality is the gap. We lead on fast, reliable delivery (+9 pts vs. competitors) but trail on "quality that lasts" (−6), which is the single strongest driver of preference.
Competitor C is closing in. Its preference share rose from 5.0% to 6.8% over four waves and is now within half a point of ours.
Recommendation: build the H2 brand platform around durability and materials proof, not only speed. Owner: Brand Marketing, creative brief by 15 Sep.

01 Awareness grew 6 points in a year, matched only by Competitor C
Aided awareness among US online home-goods shoppers has climbed every wave, from 38% to 44%. Competitor A is flat near 82%, Competitor B at 55%. Competitor C is also growing, by the same 6 points, from a smaller base.
The wave 3 → 4 increase (+3 pts, 95% CI +0.2 to +5.8) is the first single-wave change large enough to rule out sampling noise. It coincides with the expanded prospecting social flight in March–May. Among respondents who say they first heard of us in the last three months (n = 212), social media ads were the most common source by a wide margin.

02 Shoppers consider us, then choose someone else
Our funnel is wide at the top and narrows sharply at the bottom. 45% of those aware of us would consider us, close to the competitive average. Only 36% of those who consider us name us as their first choice.
Competitor A converts 49% of considerers into preference and Competitor C 45%. If we matched Competitor C's conversion rate, our preference share would be 9.0% instead of 7.2%. That would add roughly 1.8 points of first-choice share without gaining a single new aware shopper.

03 We win on delivery and lose on quality, and quality matters more
Shoppers who know us and a competitor rate us clearly ahead on fast, reliable delivery, which reflects the Pine Fleet investment. They rate us behind on durability and sustainability.
Derived importance (the correlation of each attribute with first-choice preference) ranks "quality that lasts" first and "fast, reliable delivery" fourth. Our strongest perception sits on a mid-ranked driver, and our biggest deficit sits on the top one. That explains much of the drop from consideration to preference: shoppers put us on the list for convenience, then choose on confidence in the product.

It isn't just perception
The quality gap shows up in our own data too. The returns root-cause analysis found quality-related reasons among the leading causes of textile returns, and durability is a recurring theme in the H1 NPS detractor verbatims . Brand creative can move perception only if the product backs it up.
04 Competitor C is gaining on us fastest
A year ago Competitor C had 5.0% first-choice share to our 6.1%. It now has 6.8% to our 7.2%. Both brands are growing, and C is growing faster.
Competitor C's gains are concentrated among 25–34-year-olds, where its preference (9.4%) is already above ours (8.1%). It leads us on "sustainable materials" by 15 points in that age group. Over four waves, the rise in C's preference (+1.8 pts, 95% CI +0.4 to +3.2) is significant. None of the individual wave-on-wave changes is.

05 Recommendations
Build the H2 brand platform around durability proof: materials, construction, warranty and long-term reviews, with speed as a supporting message rather than the headline. Owner: Brand Marketing (Carla Mendes) · Creative brief by: Sep 15, 2026
Publish verifiable sustainability claims for the core furniture range (e.g., share of FSC-certified wood) before we advertise them. Owner: Merchandising & Sustainability · Claims audit by: Oct 31, 2026
Keep prospecting social at the proposed higher level. It is our most effective awareness driver and is incremental (see the geo holdout ). Owner: Performance Marketing · Ongoing
Add a durability module and a 25–34 boost sample (n = +600) to wave 5 so we can track the quality gap and Competitor C among younger shoppers with tighter intervals. Owner: Marketing Science (Lena Kowalski) · Questionnaire lock: Aug 28, 2026
Run a quarterly competitive teardown of Competitor C covering assortment, price points, sustainability claims and delivery promise. Owner: Strategy & Insights (Maya Okafor) · First readout: Oct 2026
Methodology
Population
US adults aged 25–64 who bought home goods or furniture online in the past 12 months. Recruited from a double-opt-in online panel via Qualtrics, screened for category purchase, and weighted to US Census on age, gender, region and household income.
Sample
Wave 4: n = 2,421 completes (after removing 187 speeders and straight-liners). Waves 1–3: 2,412 / 2,398 / 2,405. The questionnaire has been identical across waves. The brand list rotates randomly.
Measures
Aided awareness (brand logo and name shown), consideration ("would you consider…" for next purchase over $100), first-choice preference, and a pick-any attribute association grid. Derived importance is the point-biserial correlation of each attribute with first-choice preference, among respondents aware of at least two brands.
Significance
95% margins of error use a design effect of 1.15 for weighting. Wave-on-wave tests are two-sample tests of proportions. We call a change "significant" only at p < 0.05. With four brands and several metrics per wave, expect about one false positive per wave by chance.
Limitations
Online panel respondents skew more digitally engaged than the general population, which probably inflates awareness for online-only brands, us included. Self-reported source of awareness is subject to recall bias. Competitors are anonymised in this report per Legal guidance; the key is available on request from Marketing Science.
Competitor A is a large online generalist, Competitor B a premium omnichannel furniture brand, and Competitor C a direct-to-consumer brand founded in 2021.

Design brief · October 2026
Product Development
Cat-a-Comb: our cats already chose this bed, so let's build it
A cat bed that is also a tunnel: a rectangular wood frame around a removable U-shaped foam cradle. Our cats found the shape themselves in an improvised version; this brief proposes three designs and a prototype plan.
By A. Montecalvo
Published Oct 7, 2026
Stage Concept → prototype
The short version
The cats came first. Our cats love an improvised setup: a foam mat folded into a U inside the low wooden frame under a coffee table, and a gap walled in by books. We didn't design it; they chose it.
Cat-a-Comb turns that into a product: a rectangular wood frame holding a removable U-shaped memory-foam core with a washable liner, open at both ends so it works as a bed and a tunnel.
Three variants are sketched: the Open Cradle and the Closed Tunnel (both 24″ × 10″ × 10″), and the Bibliophile's Burrow , built into a bookshelf (36″ × 10″ × 14″).
The ask: approve working prototypes of the two simplest variants and a home trial with other cats. We'd answer the open questions on materials, cleaning, safety and cost before any production decision.

01 Our cats picked this shape before we designed it
Neither setup below was built for cats. Both are improvised from what was lying around, and both get used.
The first is a soft foam mat folded into a U and wedged into the low wooden frame under a coffee table. The second is a narrow gap in the same kind of frame, walled in by upright books. Two different cats settle into them.
The improvised version: a wood frame, soft walls on both sides, a curved floor

What the cats are telling us
Walls on both sides. They choose a narrow space they can press against, not an open cushion.
A curved, padded floor. The folded mat makes a cradle that holds the body.
Cover overhead, with views out. Both spots sit under a table, with sight lines out of both open ends.
A frame that holds its shape. The wood keeps the soft walls upright. That's what the product has to replicate.
02 The concept: a wood frame around a removable U-shaped foam core
The first sketch captured the whole idea in three labels: foam interior , wood frame , cat . The concept work refined it into parts that can actually be built.
From the first sketch: foam interior inside a wood frame
Original hand sketch
[Image: Hand-drawn pen sketch on lined paper: a long rectangular wood frame with a U-shaped foam interior, labelled 'Foam interior' and 'Wood frame', and a second view showing a cat inside the tunnel, labelled 'Cat'.]
Sketch Labels: foam interior, wood frame, cat.
Anatomy of a Cat-a-Comb (as shown in the concept drawings)
| | Part | Material (proposed) | What it does
| Frame | Solid walnut rails with corner brace joints and base stabilisers | Holds the foam walls upright, and looks like furniture rather than a pet accessory
| Core | Dense memory foam, U-profile, removable | The cradle: walls on both sides and a curved floor
| Liner | Removable fabric (soft fabric or faux fur options) | Comfort, and washable
| Side panels (optional) | Clear acrylic sheets ×2 | Lets owners see the cat; keeps the foam in place
| Roof (Closed Tunnel only) | Solid walnut panel, non-transparent | Turns the bed into a covered retreat; the top doubles as a small surface
03 Three variants, from simplest to most ambitious
All three share the same idea: a wood frame and a removable U-shaped core. They differ in how enclosed the cat is and how much the piece doubles as furniture.

3 · Bibliophile's Burrow: the tunnel built into a bookshelf, with real books as the walls
Concept render · 36″ L × 10″ W × 14″ H (shelf length)
[Image: Concept render of the Bibliophile's Burrow variant: a walnut bookshelf with a U-shaped memory foam core lined with soft faux fur at one end, where a ginger-and-white cat sits, and rows of real books forming the long side walls of the tunnel. Labelled 36 inches long, 10 wide and 14 high.]
Concept render Directly inspired by the book-walls photo above. Illustrative only.
How the variants compare
| | Variant | Size (L × W × H) | Enclosure | Build complexity | Best for
| Open Cradle | 24″ × 10″ × 10″ | Open top, both ends open | Lowest | First prototype; cats who like to watch the room
| Closed Tunnel | 24″ × 10″ × 10″ | Roofed, both ends open | Low one extra panel | Shy cats; homes that want a usable top surface
| Bibliophile's Burrow | 36″ × 10″ × 14″ | Walled by books, ends open | Higher a shelf, not a bed | A statement furniture piece; later, once the core design is proven
04 Why it could be a good product, and what is still a hypothesis
The behaviour is real. Everything about the market is still to be tested.
Furniture, not a pet accessory. A walnut frame sits in a living room the way most plastic and plush cat beds don't.
Two products in one. It's a bed and a tunnel, and the Closed Tunnel adds a small surface on top.
Built for real homes. The foam core and liner come out for washing, and worn parts can be replaced without replacing the frame.
Simple to make. A frame, a foam core and two optional panels. That suggests modest tooling and a flat-pack-friendly design.
What this brief does not claim
The evidence is two of our own cats. We haven't yet tested other cats, costs, pricing, demand or manufacturing. Those are the next steps, not findings.
05 What we need to learn before deciding to make them
| | Question | Why it matters | How we'd answer it
| Do other cats use it? | Two cats is a strong signal, not proof | A home trial: lend prototypes to colleagues with cats and record use
| Is 10″ wide enough? | Large breeds may not fit, or may not feel held | Test with a range of cat sizes; consider a wider model
| Which foam, and how does it clean? | Durability against claws, odour, washability | Sample two or three foam densities and liner fabrics

Two-arm randomised controlled test (CHK-212), 50/50 split, randomised at the customer level, with device ID as the fallback for guests. Methodology
Population
2.30M customers with at least one net-positive order in the 12 months to Mar 31, 2026 (the canonical active customer ). Excludes trade/B2B accounts, employees and unmatched marketplace orders (about 3% of marketplace revenue).
Features
12 standardised features: log recency, log frequency and log net spend (RFM); share of spend in four category groups; share of orders by web, app and marketplace; share of units bought on promotion; and share of spend in big & bulky items. Pine+ status and demographics were left out deliberately.
Method
K-means with k-means++ initialisation, 50 restarts. We evaluated k = 4–9 using silhouette score (0.31 at k = 6, against 0.33 at k = 4 and 0.27 at k = 8), the elbow in within-cluster variance, and a workshop with CRM, Merchandising and Membership to check the segments were useful in practice. Stability was measured with the adjusted Rand index across 100 bootstrap samples.
Limitations
K-means favours clusters of similar size and spherical shape, so segment boundaries are approximate. Customers near a boundary (about 9%) are flagged with segment_confidence = 'low' . Methodology
Population
US promotional email subscribers who were active (at least one open or click in the last 365 days) on 25 Aug 2025: 1.60M. We drew 450,017 at random and randomised them 1:1:1 to arms, stratified by engagement tier and Pine+ status. Transactional and Pine+ lifecycle emails were unchanged.
Period
Test 1 Sep–23 Nov 2025 (12 weeks, ending before Black Friday). Follow-up 24 Nov 2025–25 Jan 2026 (9 weeks), with all arms on the standard 3/wk cadence.
Treatment
Arms received the same campaign calendar. The 2/wk arm got the two highest-priority sends each week, and the 4/wk and 6/wk arms added the next priorities in order. Content was held constant.
Analysis
Intention-to-treat on all randomised recipients, including those who later unsubscribed. We compared revenue per recipient with Welch's t-test, winsorised at the 99.9th percentile, and computed CIs by bootstrap (2,000 resamples). The annual projection scales the 12-week gain by 52/12 and assumes the tier mix stays stable.
Limitations
Autumn test period, so the effect may differ in peak or January. Tier-level estimates are subgroup analyses: they were pre-registered, but each tier has less power than the full test. We can't observe revenue lost when customers mark email as spam without unsubscribing. Unsubscribes are a lower bound on list damage.

How we run experiments: decide before you look
The Parcel & Pine experimentation playbook: pre-registration, power, guardrails, peeking, when to use a holdout or a geo test, and the one-page decision memo.
By Priya Natarajan
Published Jan 20, 2026
Applies to all product, CRM and pricing tests
The short version
Write the decision rule before launch. Every test gets a pre-registration: one primary metric, guardrails with margins, the MDE and a fixed end date.
Size tests for the effect you would act on, not the one you hope for. At our 3.4% site conversion, detecting a 2% lift takes about 1.1M sessions per arm. Most squads should plan for 5%.
Don't stop early on a good-looking result. Guardrails can stop a test at any time. The primary metric is read once, at the end.
Every test ends in a decision memo, including tests that find nothing.
01 Pre-register: the decision rule comes first
Most bad experiment calls we have reviewed came from choosing the metric after the data arrived, not from bad statistics.
Before any test goes live, the owning squad and an Insights partner fill in a pre-registration in the insights-analysis repo (template: templates/experiment_preregistration.md ). It takes about 30 minutes and records:
Hypothesis in one sentence: “Collapsing checkout to one page will increase session conversion because it removes two page loads on mobile.”
Primary metric , exactly one, with its warehouse definition (e.g. dw.fct_checkout_sessions.converted ).
Guardrail metrics , each with a tolerance, for example “AOV must not fall more than 3%”.
Unit of randomisation (customer, session, store or DMA) and the population.
MDE, power and duration , and the end date.
Pre-declared segments : at most two, chosen for a product reason.
Decision rule : what we do if the result is a win, a loss, or inconclusive.
The pre-registration is committed before launch. After launch it can only be changed by appending a dated note, never by editing it.
02 Power and MDE: small effects need very large tests
The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest true lift the test can reliably detect. Required sample size grows with the inverse square of the MDE, so halving the MDE takes four times the traffic.
Detecting a 2% lift takes 25× the traffic of detecting a 10% lift
Sessions needed per arm, baseline conversion 3.4%, α = 0.05 two-sided, 80% power · sessions
[Chart: column]
Sessions per arm: 2% MDE 1116000; 3% MDE 496000; 5% MDE 178000; 10% MDE 44600
Normal approximation, n ≈ 15.7 · p(1−p) / (p · MDE)². CUPED typically cuts these figures by 15–25%. Calculator: tools/power/mde_calculator.py .
For scale: web and app together see about 600k checkout-eligible sessions in a typical off-peak four weeks. A 50/50 test on all of that traffic can reliably detect about a 3.5% lift once CUPED is applied. Tests on a single platform or a single category page usually cannot. If the MDE you can afford is bigger than any effect you would realistically expect, the test will not tell you anything. Change the design (a broader population, a more sensitive metric, a longer run), or make the decision without a test and say so.
We use CUPED (variance reduction using each customer's pre-period behaviour) by default for customer-randomised tests. It is free power.
03 Guardrails protect the business; the primary metric decides
Guardrails are the metrics a change must not damage. Every test includes the standard set below, plus any that are specific to the test.
Standard guardrails
| | Guardrail | Default tolerance | Monitored
| Sample ratio (assignment split) | p < 0.001 on χ² stops the test | Daily, automatic
| Payment / checkout error rate | +1 pp absolute stops the test | Daily, automatic
| Average order value | −3% non-inferiority margin | At readout
| Support contacts per 1k orders | +10% | Weekly
| Page performance (p75 load time) | +200 ms | Daily
04 Peeking: look at guardrails any time, and at the primary metric once
If you check a fixed-horizon test every day and stop the first time p < 0.05, the real false-positive rate over four weeks is closer to 25% than 5%.
The experiment dashboard hides the primary-metric result until the pre-registered end date. If a squad genuinely needs to be able to stop early (a risky pricing change, or a launch tied to a date), we design the test as a sequential test from the start. We use group-sequential boundaries (O'Brien–Fleming) with up to three planned looks. This costs about 10% more sample. What we will not do is turn a fixed test into a sequential one after launch.
“But it's clearly winning”
In 2025 we reviewed 14 tests that looked like clear winners at week 1. Five of them were flat or negative by the planned end date. Early novelty effects, weekday mix and a single big order can all create a week-1 “win”.
05 A/B test, holdout or geo test?
Randomising customers is the gold standard, but it is not always possible or sufficient. Use this table to pick the design, and ask in #insights-help if you are unsure.
Choosing a design
| | Design | Use when | Example | Watch out for
| A/B test | You can randomise individual customers or sessions and the effect shows up within weeks. | Checkout layout, search ranking, email subject lines | Spill-over between arms (shared carts, households)
| Holdout | A feature is already live and you want its ongoing incremental value, or you need to measure long-run effects. | Recommendation carousel, Pine+ perks, lifecycle emails | Holdout customers get a worse experience, so keep it small (5–10%) and time-boxed or rotating
| Geo test | The treatment cannot be targeted at individuals, such as media, pricing seen in public, or delivery promises. | Paid social spend, TV, Pine Fleet delivery windows | Few units (DMAs), so you need synthetic control and pre-period matching; allow 6–10 weeks
06 Every test ends in a one-page decision memo
Inconclusive tests are results too. Writing them up stops the same idea being retested in six months.
The memo template ( templates/decision_memo.md ) has seven headings, in this order:
Decision : ship, don't ship, or iterate, in one line at the top.
What we tested and why : two sentences, with a link to the pre-registration.
Primary result : absolute and relative effect with a 95% CI, stated as a sentence and not only as a p-value.
Guardrails : a table with a pass, watch or fail read for each.
Pre-declared segments : results for those segments only. Anything else is labelled exploratory.
Expected impact : the annualised figure and the planning figure after a haircut. Our rule of thumb is to plan on 40–60% of the point estimate, because winning tests shrink after rollout.
Next steps : each with an owner and a date.
The memo is posted in #experiments and filed in the Insights Hub. Longer write-ups are welcome, but the decision memo is required.

Methodology
Population
All 2,140 hourly FC associates hired into permanent or seasonal-to-permanent roles from Jan 1, 2025 to Mar 31, 2026 at Reno, Dallas, Columbus and Allentown. Agency temps, rehires within 12 months and internal transfers are excluded.
Outcome
Separation of any kind (resignation, job abandonment or termination) within 90 days of start date. Involuntary terminations are 9% of the 818 exits. Excluding them does not change the pattern of findings.
Risk factors
Schedule changes come from wfm.fct_shift_assignments (a change is any involuntary shift or day change posted less than 7 days ahead). Trainer ratio is new starters per certified trainer in onboarding week. Commute is drive time from home ZIP centroid to site at shift start, estimated with a routing API.
Model
Cox proportional hazards with FC and shift as strata and robust standard errors clustered by hire week. We checked the proportional-hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residuals; the schedule-change effect is strongest in weeks 1–3.
Privacy
Analysis is at aggregate level only. No group with fewer than 10 people is reported, and exit-interview verbatims were not used in this report.
Limitations
This is an observational study. Short-notice schedule changes may partly reflect sites that are under strain in other ways, which is why we propose testing rather than rolling out. Commute distance uses home ZIP code, not actual travel mode. Exit-interview coverage is 38%, and response is skewed towards resignations.

Methodology
Population
Treated group: non-member sessions and orders on web and app (US). Control: orders placed through marketplace channels, which are not subject to our free-shipping threshold. Pine+ members were excluded from the treated group, since their shipping is always free. A secondary check using members as a control gave similar AOV (+12.1%) and conversion (−7.3%) estimates.
Period
Pre-period 5 Jan–1 Mar 2026 (8 weeks). Post-period 2 Mar–5 Apr 2026 (5 weeks). Presidents' Day week was kept in, since it affected both groups similarly.
Method
Difference-in-differences on weekly metrics with week and channel fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by week, and 95% CIs come from a wild-cluster bootstrap. For bunching, we compared the observed basket-value distribution against a smoothed counterfactual fitted outside the $65–95 window.
Limitations
(1) Five post-weeks is short. Novelty effects may fade, and long-run customer loss isn't observed yet. (2) Marketplace shoppers differ from our web and app shoppers, so the control handles seasonality and demand shocks but not differences in customer mix. (3) The St. Patrick's Day textile promotion (16–22 Mar) ran on web and app only. Excluding that week moves the AOV estimate by less than 0.3 pts. (4) Contribution figures use average margins and could differ at the SKU level.

Methodology
Population
955 employees assigned to an office in Workday (Denver 780, Chicago 175). Remote employees and visitors are excluded from per-employee measures but included in the desk counts (about 3% of daily badge-ins).
Period
Jan 5 – Mar 13, 2026: 10 weeks, 48 working days after excluding two company holidays.
Utilisation
Unique people per day with a badge-in, divided by the number of assignable desks. A cross-check against desk check-ins agreed within 2 points, since most people who badge in also check in to a desk.
Co-presence
For each person-day in the office, whether at least 50% of their Workday team (same manager, teams of 10 or more) also badged in that day. Averaged per person, then per team.

612 pulse respondents; 488 consented to linkage. Results are shown only for groups of 10 or more. People Analytics performed the linkage, and badge data was never shown to managers at individual level.

Badge data misses tailgating (estimated 2–4% of entries). We have one quarter of data and seasonality is estimated from 2025. People who consented to linkage may differ from those who did not: their overall attendance was 0.2 days a week higher.

Only Pine Fleet meets the 95% on-time promise, and padding our delivery dates has hidden how far carriers have slipped
On-time delivery across the network was 92.1% from January to August. Adding buffer days to the promise made the headline number look better, cost us conversion and left the late tail where it was.
By Tom Becker
Published Sep 4, 2026
Data through Aug 31, 2026
The short version
Only Pine Fleet meets the SLA. Our in-house fleet delivered 96.4% of parcels by the promised date. National carriers managed 90.8% and white-glove partners 84.1%, so the network as a whole reached 92.1% against a 95% target.
The gap comes from the carriers, not the metros. In the same six metros and the same ZIP codes, Pine Fleet beats the national carriers by 3.9 to 5.8 pp.
Padding the promise hid a ~4 pp decline in carrier performance. Since March we have added a buffer day on 38% of national-carrier volume. Measured against their unpadded transit standard, the carriers fell from 92.1% to 86.0%. The padded lanes also lost 1.2% of checkout conversion (≈$3.6M a year).
Late parcels cost us NPS. Late deliveries are 7.9% of parcels but 23% of transactional-NPS detractors. When a parcel is two or more days late, NPS drops from +52 to −8.
Recommendation: remove padding lane by lane, hold carriers to scan-based SLAs with penalties, and grow Pine Fleet ZIP coverage in Chicago and Philadelphia first. Owners: Delivery Experience, Transportation, CX Ops.

01 Pine Fleet has stayed above 95% all year. National carriers and white-glove have both drifted down since March
The network missed the 95% SLA in every month of 2026. Pine Fleet cleared it every month, including the July Pine Days peak. The two partner channels are moving the wrong way.
From January to August we delivered 7.08M parcels: 2.19M by Pine Fleet (31%), 4.46M by national carriers (63%) and 0.43M big-and-bulky shipments by white-glove partners (6%). Pine Fleet's monthly on-time rate stayed between 95.8% and 96.9%. The national carriers fell from 92.4% in January to 88.9% in July and recovered only to 90.1% in August. White-glove fell further, from 86.2% to a low of 82.7% in June. Because national carriers carry nearly two-thirds of our volume, their slide drives the network number. A 1 pp change in carrier on-time moves the network by about 0.6 pp.

02 Carriers are 4–6 pp behind Pine Fleet even on the same streets
One explanation for Pine Fleet's lead would be that it only serves dense, easy metros. The data doesn't support that.
National carriers still deliver about 18% of parcels inside the six Pine Fleet metros, either as overflow or for ZIPs at the edge of fleet coverage. When we compare the two channels on the same metro, ZIP-code ring and parcel size class, Pine Fleet is ahead by 3.9 to 5.8 pp. Chicago and Philadelphia have the largest gaps and are also the two metros where Pine Fleet is itself closest to the SLA line. The cause is capacity. Fleet routes there are at 94–97% of planned stops on Mondays, so some Monday overflow goes to carriers, and those overflow parcels are late 11% of the time.

03 Padding the promise lifted the headline rate by ~4 pp and hid the carriers' decline
From March, the Delivery Promise team added one buffer day to national-carrier lanes that had missed 92% in the previous four weeks. That rule now applies to 38% of national-carrier volume.
The padding did what it was designed to do on paper. In the padded lanes, on-time against the customer promise rose by 2.1 pp in the first month. It did not change carrier performance. When we measure the same parcels against the carrier's unpadded scan-based transit standard (the date we would have promised without the buffer), national-carrier on-time fell from 92.1% in January to 86.0% in August. Against the padded promise the fall was only to 90.1%. The ~4 pp difference is decline we stopped seeing.

Padding also has a cost that the delivery dashboards don't show. A longer promise at checkout loses orders. We compared padded lanes with similar unpadded lanes before and after March (difference-in-differences, weekly lane panels). Checkout conversion in padded lanes fell by 1.2% relative (95% CI −0.4% to −2.0%). Padded lanes carry about 24% of our orders, so the loss is roughly $3.6M in annualised revenue . That is about what Transportation would pay out in a year of late-delivery credits on the same parcels.
Why padding can't fix this
A buffer day helps only when a parcel is exactly one day late. In 2026, 61% of our late parcels were two or more days late. Most of those are lost-in-network, sort-centre missorts and failed first attempts, and one extra day would not have saved them. The padding moved the promise date, but the late parcels are still late.
04 Late parcels are 8% of deliveries and 23% of detractors
We linked 61,200 transactional NPS responses to the delivery outcome of the order they rated.
Customers whose parcel arrived on time gave an NPS of +52. One day late brought it down to +31, and two or more days late to −8. Late parcels make up 7.9% of deliveries (3.1% one day late, 4.8% two or more), but because the detractor rate for 2+-days-late orders is 41%, they account for about 23% of all delivery-related detractors. This matches the "late and no update" theme in the H1 NPS verbatim analysis . There, customers were more upset about how little they were told than about the delay.

In most networks, reliability costs extra. Here the cheaper channel is also the more reliable one.
In its metros Pine Fleet costs $6.85 per parcel, fully loaded (drivers, vans, fuel, sort labour, depot lease). National carriers cost $7.60 on average, before peak and residential surcharges. One definition each for active customer, active member, retained member and churn
The canonical definitions behind our customer and Pine+ metrics, how each is calculated, the edge cases, and why two dashboards can show different numbers on the same day.
By Jonah Feld
Published Feb 10, 2026
Applies from Q1 2026 reporting
The short version
Active customer means at least one net-positive order shipped in the trailing 365 days. On Jan 31, 2026 there were 2.29M.
Active member means a Pine+ member who has benefits on the as-of date. This includes the payment-retry grace period and gifted memberships, and excludes free trials. On Jan 31, 2026 there were 463,200.
Churn is counted on the date access ends , not the date someone clicks cancel, and is always split into voluntary and involuntary.
If your dashboard shows a different number, check the table in section 04 before raising a data-quality ticket.
01 Why we need one definition
In January the Exec KPI deck, the Membership Ops dashboard and the CRM team each reported a different Pine+ member count for the same week. The largest and smallest were about 25,000 apart. None of them was wrong. Each answered a slightly different question. But a VP seeing three numbers can’t tell which one to plan with, and FP&A had to reconcile them by hand every month.
These definitions are now built once in dbt ( fct_member_status_daily and fct_customer_activity_daily ) and every certified dashboard reads from those models. If you calculate these metrics yourself, use the models rather than rebuilding the logic.
02 The definitions
Active customer
A customer is active on a date if they had at least one net-positive order shipped in the 365 days up to and including that date. Net-positive means the order was not fully cancelled or fully returned. A customer who bought a lamp and returned it still counts if they kept anything else from that order.
In prose SQL: take shipped orders from dw.fct_orders where net revenue after returns is greater than zero, keep those with a ship date in the window, remove test, employee and trade (B2B) accounts using dw.dim_customer , and count distinct customer_id .
Marketplace orders count only when matched to a known customer (68% of marketplace orders). Unmatched marketplace buyers are not in the count.
Guest checkouts are merged onto an account by email. Two emails means two customers, even if it is the same household.
Ship date, not order date. A pre-order placed in December and shipped in February counts from February.
Active member
A customer is an active member on a date if their Pine+ subscription gives them benefits on that date. That includes:
paid monthly and annual members, including those who have cancelled but are still inside the period they paid for (they still get free shipping, so they are still members);
members in the 14-day payment retry (“grace”) window after a failed charge;
gifted and partner-bundled memberships.
It excludes free trials . Trialists are counted separately as trial_members because about 40% never pay, and counting them would inflate membership every time Growth runs a trial campaign. Employee memberships are also excluded.
Retained member
A member is retained over a period if they were an active member at the start and are still one at the end. Retention rate is retained members divided by active members at the start. People who join during the period are left out of both the numerator and the denominator, so a big sign-up month cannot make retention look better.
A member who churns and re-joins within the period counts as retained only if they are active on the end date. We flag these as is_rejoin = true so they can be excluded when that matters, for example in cohort survival curves.
Churn: voluntary and involuntary
A member churns on the first day they no longer have benefits. Monthly churn rate is members who churned during the month divided by active members at the start of the month. We always report the two types separately:
Voluntary churn: the member cancelled, or turned off auto-renew, and their paid period ran out.
Involuntary churn: a renewal charge failed and was still failing at the end of the 14-day retry window. The churn date is the end of the grace period.
In January 2026, total monthly churn was 3.1%: 2.4% voluntary and 0.7% involuntary. These are all-plan figures. Monthly-plan churn runs much higher than annual.
The cancel-click trap
An annual member who cancels in March but paid through November churns in November . Dashboards built on cancellation events from the app will show that churn eight months early. The cancel click is still useful as a leading indicator of intent, so it is available as cancel_requested_at . Just don’t call it churn.
03 Edge cases we’ve already decided
Edge-case rulings
| | Situation | Ruling
| Member switches monthly → annual | Not churn. Same membership, new plan_type from the switch date.
| Member pauses (up to 3 months) | Not active while paused, and not churned. Counted as paused_members .
| Refund within the 30-day guarantee | Churn (voluntary), dated to the refund date. The member is removed from “active” on that date.
| Charge fails, then succeeds on day 9 | Never churned. Active throughout.
| Rejoins within 90 days of churning | A new membership spell with is_rejoin = true . The original churn still counts.
| Time zone | All dates in America/Denver (company time), not UTC.
04 Why your dashboard shows a different number
Most “data discrepancies” reported to #insights-help are dashboards using a different definition. On Jan 31, 2026, four common sources gave four different member counts:

Billing (452.9k) counts successfully charged subscriptions. It leaves out the grace window (≈6,100) and gifted or partner memberships (≈4,200).
Membership Ops (471.9k) adds free trialists (≈8,700).
CRM (478.4k) keeps anyone flagged as a member at any point in the last 30 days, so recent churners stay on the list for a month.
Other common causes: refresh lag (billing syncs nightly, and Braze lags a further day), UTC cut-offs that move a day of activity, and an average-over-month figure compared with an end-of-month figure.
What to use
For anything that goes to leadership, FP&A or the board, use the canonical definition and label it “active members (canonical)”. If you use another definition for an operational reason, say so in the chart subtitle. Questions and proposed changes go through the #metrics-council channel. Methodology
Population

Definitions

Method
Kaplan–Meier survival curves by plan and channel; monthly hazards computed on members at risk at the start of each tenure month. Methodology
Survey
Qualtrics relationship NPS, sent quarterly to a random sample of active customers (purchased in last 12 months), stratified by member status and region. Response rate 9.4%. Results are weighted to the active-customer base.
Coding
A hybrid approach. (1) BERTopic clustering on sentence embeddings produced 22 candidate topics. (2) Two researchers merged these into an 11-theme codebook with sentiment. (3) Two coders labelled 1,500 verbatims by hand (inter-rater κ = 0.84). (4) An LLM classifier prompted with the codebook labelled the full set. Its agreement with the human labels was κ = 0.81 overall and ≥ 0.76 on every theme. A 5% sample of the classifier’s labels is audited each wave.
Linkage
Respondents were matched to their most recent delivered order before the survey date (93% match rate). Delivery status comes from carrier and Pine Fleet scan events.

Why the dashboards got this wrong

Methodology
Design
Matched-market geo holdout. We ranked 210 DMAs on 52 weeks of revenue history and paired them on trend correlation, revenue size, Pine+ penetration and Pine Fleet coverage. We kept the 14 best-matched pairs and randomised which member of each pair went dark. We excluded the 6 Pine Fleet home metros except Phoenix and Columbus, which were matched to each other. The 28 DMAs cover 19.9% of US revenue.
Period
Pre-period 9 Feb–5 Apr 2026 (8 weeks). Test 6 Apr–17 May 2026 (6 weeks). We watched a one-week cool-down to 24 May for residual effects and found none detectable after week 1 of it.
Estimation
Augmented synthetic control on weekly net revenue by DMA, with confidence intervals from placebo-in-time and placebo-in-space permutations (1,000 draws). A difference-in-differences cross-check gave 4.3% (CI 2.6–6.0%).
Hurdle rate
1.8× revenue iROAS, set by FP&A. This is contribution-margin breakeven on first-order revenue plus expected 12-month repeat revenue from new customers.
Limitations
(1) Spring seasonality only; peak may differ. (2) National brand and TV spend continued in all markets, so we measure paid social's effect on top of that baseline, not in isolation. (3) The retargeting estimate rests on 7 vs. 7 markets over 4 weeks and has a wide CI (0.21–1.73×). Even its upper bound is below the hurdle. (4) Spillover from people who live in one DMA and shop in another would bias the estimate slightly downward.
1 Prospecting incremental revenue = total holdout effect − retargeting effect, scaled to spend. The two estimates share a control group, so their CIs are not independent. We bootstrapped the blended CI directly and did not sum the tactic CIs.

Methodology
Population
All Pine+ members who joined 1 Jan 2023–30 Jun 2026 (682k joiners). Employee and gifted memberships are excluded. Members who switched plan are assigned to the plan they joined on.
LTV definition
Three-year contribution, discounted at 10% a year. It includes membership fees plus incremental order contribution (gross margin on orders above the member's matched counterfactual) minus the free-shipping subsidy and Pine Points cost. We matched each member to non-members on 12-month pre-join spend, order count, category mix and region (propensity score, 1:3 nearest neighbour).
Retention forecast
Discrete-time survival model by plan and cohort, with renewal-month effects for annual members and a month-3 effect for monthly members. It is fitted on observed months and extrapolated to month 36. Back-testing the 2023 cohort from its first 12 months predicted M30 retention within 1.8 pts.
Member base forecast
Cohort-component model: opening base, minus churn from the survival curves, plus new joins (FY27 plan traffic × join rates, adjusted by scenario). The 80% ranges come from 5,000 simulations that vary join rate, renewal rate and test-estimate uncertainty.
Limitations
(1) The 2025 and 2026 cohorts rely mainly on forecast retention. (2) Price tests were short and silent, so real-world reaction may be larger, as in the downside case. (3) Incremental order contribution assumes the matched comparison captures self-selection into membership. If members would have spent more anyway, LTV is overstated. The overstatement is likely proportional across scenarios, so the ranking of scenarios should hold. (4) We do not model competitor price responses.
Fee revenue is recognised on a cash basis here for simplicity. FP&A's plan will recognise annual fees ratably, which moves roughly $0.6M of the FY27 fee uplift into FY28 in the $65 scenario.

How to read a confidence interval, and why “significant” doesn’t mean “worth doing”
A five-minute guide for anyone who reads our experiment and survey results. No formulas.
By Priya Natarajan
Published May 6, 2026
Reading time 6 min
The short version
Read the range, not just the number. “+1.2 pp (95% CI 0.4 to 2.0)” means the true effect is probably somewhere between +0.4 and +2.0 pp. Plan with the whole range.
“Statistically significant” only means the range doesn’t include zero. It tells you nothing about whether the effect is big enough to matter.
Ask two questions: Is the effect real (the range excludes zero)? Is it worth it (the range sits above the smallest effect we’d act on)?
01 A confidence interval is a range of plausible values
Every number we report from a sample, whether an A/B test, a survey or a cohort, is an estimate. If we ran the same checkout test again next month with different customers, we would get a slightly different answer. A confidence interval (CI) shows how far that answer could reasonably move.
Suppose we write: “The new checkout lifted conversion by 1.2 pp (95% CI 0.4 to 2.0 pp).” Read it like this:
Our best single estimate is +1.2 pp .
Given the data, anything from about +0.4 pp to +2.0 pp is plausible. Values outside that range are unlikely.
“95%” describes how reliable the method is: if we repeated the test many times, about 95 in 100 of the intervals we built would contain the true effect.
In practice: when you make a decision, check that it still makes sense at both ends of the range. If the plan only works when the effect is +2.0 pp, that is a risk worth stating.
A common mix-up
A 95% CI does not mean “95% of customers fall in this range”. It is about the uncertainty in our estimate of the average , not about how much individual customers vary.
02 More data gives a narrower range, but with diminishing returns
The width of the interval depends mostly on how much data we have and how noisy the metric is. Conversion, which is a yes/no outcome, settles down quickly. Revenue per visitor, where a single sofa order can swing the average, needs much more data.
The chart shows how precise a two-arm A/B test is on a metric with a 4% baseline, similar to our web checkout conversion. To halve the width of the interval you need four times as many visitors.
Doubling precision takes four times the traffic
± half-width of the 95% CI on the difference between two arms · baseline conversion 4% · by visitors per arm
[Chart: line]
± CI half-width: 1k 1.72 pp; 5k 0.77 pp; 10k 0.54 pp; 25k 0.34 pp; 50k 0.24 pp; 100k 0.17 pp
Illustrative. Half-width = 1.96 × √(2 × 0.04 × 0.96 ⁄ n). Only past about 30k visitors per arm is the interval tight enough to separate a 0.3 pp effect from zero.
This is why the Experimentation team sometimes asks for a test to run for four weeks instead of two. It is not caution for its own sake. With less data, the interval would still include both “nothing happened” and “this is worth $2M”.
03 “Statistically significant” and “meaningful” are different questions
A result is statistically significant (at the 95% level) when its confidence interval does not include zero. That is all it means: the effect is probably not zero. It does not mean large, important or worth shipping.
Before every test we agree on a minimum meaningful effect , the smallest change that would justify the build, rollout or cost. For a checkout change this might be +0.3 pp of conversion. For a Pine+ price change it might be −1 pp of churn. Then we read the interval against both zero and that line:
Four results, read two ways (minimum meaningful effect = +0.3 pp)
| | Example | Estimate | 95% CI | Significant? | Meaningful? | How to read it
| A. Big test, tiny effect | +0.08 pp | +0.02 to +0.14 | Yes | No | Real but too small to matter. Don’t ship because it’s “significant”.
| B. Clear win | +0.9 pp | +0.5 to +1.3 | Yes | Yes | Even the low end clears the bar. Ship it.
| C. Promising but unsure | +0.6 pp | −0.1 to +1.3 | No | Maybe | Could be nothing, could be great. Get more data rather than calling it a failure.
| D. Confident “no effect” | +0.02 pp | −0.15 to +0.19 | No | No | The whole range is below the bar. A useful result: stop investing here.
Examples C and D are both “not significant”, but they lead to opposite decisions. C says we don’t know yet. D says we know it doesn’t matter. Reporting both as “no significant difference” loses that distinction, which is why our reports always show the interval and not just a verdict.
Watch for these phrases
“Trending towards significance” usually means example C. Treat it as unknown, not as a weak yes. “Highly significant (p < 0.001)” says the effect is very probably real, not that it is very big. Example A could be p < 0.001 with a large enough sample.
04 Questions to ask when you read one of our reports
What is the range, and does my decision hold at both ends? If the low end would change your mind, say so in the review.
What was the minimum meaningful effect, and was it set before the test? It should appear in the pre-registration (see the experimentation playbook ). A threshold chosen after seeing the results is not reliable.
How many comparisons were made? If we looked at 20 segments, about one will look “significant” by chance. Our reports mark any segment cut that was not pre-planned as exploratory.
Is the sample the right population? A narrow interval around the wrong group is still the wrong answer. For example, a survey of app users only tells you about app users.
If you’re unsure how to read a specific result, ask in #experimentation. We would much rather answer a question before a decision than explain a result afterwards.

The reason picker undercounts the causes we can fix
We coded a random sample of 3,850 free-text return comments. In 18% of the "changed my mind" returns, the comment actually described a description or damage problem ("smaller than I thought", "chipped on one corner"). The customer picked the easiest option. The true share of damage and description returns is therefore probably 2–4 pp higher than shown. Our savings estimates use the reason codes as recorded, so they are conservative.
03 Most damage comes from flat-pack furniture sent by carrier and fragile items on two auto-bagger lines
About 61% of damage cost is furniture ($5.70M). Most of the rest is lighting and ceramics, and both problems come down to a few specific ways we ship.
Big & bulky. About 38% of furniture units are flat-pack items that go by national carrier in a carton, not by white-glove. Those units come back damaged at 58 per 1,000 shipped. White-glove deliveries, which are blanket-wrapped and carried in by two people, come back damaged at 16.5 per 1,000. That comes to about 21.4k damaged returns and $3.9M of damage cost in H1, or 68% of all furniture damage cost. The 150 worst SKUs account for 58% of that. Most are tall case goods (bookcases, wardrobes) weighing over 70 lb, which carrier sort equipment handles badly.
Fragile goods. Lighting and glass or ceramic decor (1.62M units in H1) come back damaged at 55 per 1,000 overall. The rate depends heavily on how they are packed. Allentown Line 4 and Columbus Line 2 run automated baggers that put bubble-lined poly mailers on anything under the size limit, and that includes lamps and ceramics. Those units are damaged at 92 per 1,000, which is eight times the rate for double-wall cartons with molded-pulp inserts.

04 "Didn't match description" follows the gaps in our product photos
In the interviews, customers didn't say the product was bad. They said it wasn't what the photos had shown them.
Aisha interviewed 24 customers who had returned an item as "didn't match description" in May or June. Fourteen said the colour was different from what they expected, 11 said the item was smaller or larger than they had pictured, and 8 mentioned material or texture. Several named more than one. Nobody said the listing text was wrong. Most hadn't read it. Customers relied on the images, and the images were missing two things: a colour-accurate swatch and a shot that showed the item next to something for scale.
We then checked this against the catalogue. Using image metadata in dw.dim_product , we grouped every SKU by photo completeness. SKUs with a full set (six or more images, a scale or lifestyle shot and a colour-calibrated swatch) have a description-return rate of 1.4% of units shipped. SKUs missing only the scale shot come in at 2.6%, those missing the calibrated swatch at 3.3%, and those with three or fewer images at 3.9%. The pattern holds within each category and price band.

Methodology
Population
All units shipped Jan 1 – Jun 30, 2026 from our four FCs (8.1M) and returns initiated against them by Jul 31 (889.3k), so each shipment had a return window of at least 30 days. Marketplace-fulfilled orders are excluded.
Cost of returns
Reverse freight, returns processing labour (from Workday time allocated to returns), inventory write-down for non-resaleable units, and replacement shipments. Customer refunds are not counted as a cost.
Quantitative
Descriptive rates by reason, category, pack spec and photo completeness. For photo effects, a logistic regression of description returns on image features with category, price band and FC controls.
Qualitative
24 semi-structured remote interviews (45 min) by Aisha Rahman, May 27 – Jun 20, 2026, recruited from recent description returners across all categories. Also 3,850 randomly sampled free-text return comments, double-coded (κ = 0.81).
Savings
H1 volumes × expected change in rate × cost per return, doubled for a full year. Implementation costs from Packaging Engineering and Creative Studio quotes.
Limitations
Reason codes are self-reported and noisy (see section 2). Photo completeness is correlated with SKU age and vendor, which we control for only in part. Interview participants are self-selected and are not a representative sample.

The short version
Pick productivity varies widely by site. Reno averaged 62 units per labour hour (UPH) from January to April. Dallas averaged 55, Columbus 51 and Allentown 46. The network averaged 53.

This isn't about Allentown's people
The GM, and some of the site review decks, have put Allentown's gap down to "a newer, greener workforce". Tenure does matter, since a new picker is 14 UPH slower than a one-year veteran. But Allentown's extra share of new pickers explains only 1.8 of the 16 UPH gap. If Allentown had Reno's tenure mix tomorrow and kept its current slotting and batching, it would still be the slowest site.
03 Batching is the cheapest lever, and it stops paying off at about 12 orders
Allentown's carts carry 6.4 orders on average and Reno's carry 11.2. Allentown's small batches come from a wave-release setting, not from any physical limit.
Each extra order on the cart spreads the walk across more units. The effect is strong up to about 12 orders, after which cart capacity and sort-at-pack errors take most of the gain away. At Reno, batches above 12 had a 0.9% mis-sort rate compared with 0.3% below 12. Changing Allentown's and Columbus's wave release rule to a 10–12 order target is a WMS configuration change and needs no capital.

Reno ramps new pickers faster than the other sites. In a new picker's fourth week Reno measures 47 UPH, compared with 41 at Allentown. Reno pairs each new hire with a "pick buddy" for the first two weeks and starts them on single-zone batches before moving them onto full paths. 05 Moving Allentown and Columbus halfway to Reno's practices would save ~21,800 pick hours a year
We do not assume either site can match Reno completely. Reno's building has a single-level pick module, while Allentown's has a mezzanine. Our target is for each site to close half its gap to Reno. That means Allentown from 46 to 54 UPH and Columbus from 51 to 56.5. At January–April volumes this saves 3,800 hours at Allentown and 2,300 at Columbus, or 6,100 hours in four months. January–April is about 28% of annual unit volume, so the annual saving is about 21,800 hours, or $0.53M at a $24.50 loaded rate . Nearly half of that saving would come in November and December, when each hour saved is an hour we don't have to fill with a temp.
Caveat
The model shows association at the shift level, and slotting is not randomly assigned. Before scaling, we recommend a controlled pilot: re-slot one Allentown zone and use the other zones as the comparison.

Methodology
Population
All each-pick tasks at the four FCs, Jan 5 – Apr 30, 2026 (5.22M units; 212,400 associate-shifts; 1,062 distinct pickers). Excludes big-and-bulky (team-lift) picks, replenishment and returns put-away.
Metric
UPH = units picked ÷ pick labour hours. Pick hours include direct task time plus a pro-rata share of indirect time (start-up meetings, cart staging) from Workday time clocks.
Model
Linear mixed model of shift-level UPH with associate random intercepts. Fixed effects: golden-zone share of the shift's picks, mean travel per pick (from WMS location coordinates), batch size (piecewise, knot at 12), tenure band, category mix, units per order, shift and week. Decomposition = coefficient × Reno–Allentown difference in each driver's mean.
Validation
Out-of-sample R² on May 1–10 data was 0.58. The site ranking and the size of the effects were stable when the model was fitted to each FC separately.
Limitations
Observational: better-run sites may also do other things well that we haven't measured. Travel distance is estimated from bin coordinates, not measured. Building constraints (Allentown's mezzanine) are grouped under "unexplained".
